rationale: B wins because it finds the harder, more reportable story inside the announcement: "Substack says its top creators split more than $400M last year — and won't say how the split works." That is a real reporter-shaped question with a denominator problem, proof demands, and a desk that would care. A has usable bones, but "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" overstates the facts before the reporting even starts. That's how you turn a decent angle into a correction waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" is not grounded. The update says native video is launching and Substack has leaned into a media-app strategy; it does not say the swap is complete or all-in on video.
"short-form, algorithmic-style feed" decorates the supplied "TikTok-style feed" with mechanics the update does not give. Ask whether it is algorithmic; do not assert it.
"The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up" overreaches. Creator earnings and 4 million paid subscriptions do not, by themselves, answer Substack's funding problem.
The category angle and YouTube/TikTok angle overlap, and the two funding angles recycle the same viability frame from opposite sides. Distinct enough to workshop, not clean enough to ship.
gaps_in_B: "Substack has stopped competing with Mailchimp and started competing with YouTube" imports Mailchimp and overstates the category break. Strong line, but a little too pleased with itself.

"writers ... face a feed that rewards something they didn't sign up to make" assumes pressure and distribution effects not in the facts. The proof section catches this, but the angle headline still leans ahead of the evidence.

"Video hosting is one of the most expensive infrastructure commitments a platform can make" is plausible, but it is outside the supplied update. Source it before letting that become the spine of the finance pitch.
